subtype: Reading tone in text without voice [Interpreting]
passage: I'm Nazia, and I once spent an entire evening hurt by one word. My group-project partner Bidisha had messaged me, "Fine." That was all. I'd asked if she could send her slides by Thursday, and she wrote "Fine." No emoji, no exclamation, no "sure!" like she usually sent. I read it as anger. I stared at the screen for an hour, drafting a cold reply, then deleting it. Finally I called her instead. She picked up on the first ring, sounding out of breath. "Sorry, I was on the bus in the rain, I could only type one word! Slides tomorrow, promise." I sat there feeling silly and relieved. Now, when a message sounds cold, I try to ask before I decide it is.

qa.q: What single word did Bidisha send?
qa.a: She sent "Fine."

qa.q: What did Nazia feel when she read the word, and what was the actual reason for its brevity?
qa.a: Nazia felt hurt, reading it as anger, but Bidisha was simply on a rainy bus and could type only one word.

qa.q: What could Nazia do the next time a message seems cold?
qa.a: Nazia could ask a quick clarifying question or call, instead of guessing the mood from a short text.

qa.q: How might Bidisha have felt when Nazia called?
qa.a: Bidisha was probably surprised and apologetic, as she was out of breath and hadn't realised how her one word sounded.

grounding: Nazia misreads a rushed, brief text as anger and checks by calling.

subtype: Reading tone in text without voice [Interpreting]
passage: Counsellor's note, Thursday. Akash came in upset about an email from his lab supervisor, Jahnavi, that read only: "Send me the data. Now." He had taken it as anger and was rehearsing what to say to withdraw from the project. I asked what else could explain the message. He listed a few: she might be rushed, or on her phone, or in a meeting. We agreed the email itself did not tell us her tone. I suggested he reply briefly and ask, "Do you need the raw file or the summary, and by when?" That gives her something easy to answer. He did, and she answered within a minute: raw file, before her flight. Akash relaxed and said he should have checked first. I will note that his worry was understandable.

qa.q: What did Jahnavi's email say?
qa.a: It said, "Send me the data. Now."

qa.q: What did Akash believe about the email at first, and what did the counsellor help him see?
qa.a: He believed Jahnavi was angry, and the counsellor helped him see that the short wording could also mean she was rushed or busy.

qa.q: What could Akash do in future when a message seems curt?
qa.a: He could reply with a short, specific question, or call, to check what the sender needs instead of assuming anger.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi have seen her own message?
qa.a: She probably wrote it quickly because she was rushing to catch a flight, and may not have realised it could sound harsh.

grounding: A counsellor helps Akash see that a curt email may simply be rushed and to check before assuming anger.

subtype: Reading tone in text without voice [Interpreting]
passage:
Wednesday night.
Sent Tanvir a long message this afternoon about changing our trip dates, with three options and a joke. The reply came an hour later: "k."
Just "k." With a full stop.
My stomach knotted. Is Tanvir angry? Last week I cancelled on the movie. Maybe this is payback. I typed three long replies and deleted all of them. I couldn't focus on my assignment.
At nine I just called. Tanvir picked up, sounding cheerful. "Hey! Sorry, I was in the lab all day, typing with gloves on. 'k' meant okay, option two is perfect." I laughed from relief. I told Tanvir about my three deleted replies and we both laughed more.
Note to self: a short message is usually a busy person, not an angry one. And a call takes thirty seconds.
— Nitin

qa.q: What was Tanvir's reply?
What was Nitin feeling after reading "k."?
qa.a: Nitin felt anxious and unsettled, stomach knotted, worrying Tanvir was angry about the cancelled movie.

qa.q: What did Nitin do that cleared things up?
qa.a: Nitin called instead of guessing, which quickly showed the reply was just rushed.

qa.q: Why was Tanvir's reply so short?
qa.a: Tanvir had been in the lab all day typing with gloves on, so "k" simply meant okay, option two.

grounding: Shows a young adult misreading a short text as anger and learning, through a call, that it was just rushed.

subtype: Reading tone in text without voice [Interpreting]
passage: Rukmini had worked at the panchayat office in Kallur for only two weeks when her phone buzzed at seven in the morning. It was from Lokesh, the secretary. "Come to office. Now." Her heart raced. Had she made a mistake in the ration lists? She hadn't even had tea. She walked fast through the lanes, rehearsing apologies. At the office she found Lokesh on the phone, shouting over a bad line, surrounded by files. He waved her in, covered the phone and said, "Thank god. The district officer is coming at nine, and you're the only one who knows the new computer system. Can you print the lists?" Rukmini let out a long breath. "I thought I was in trouble!" Lokesh looked puzzled. "Why?" She showed him the message. He laughed. "I typed with one thumb while the officer was on the other line. Sorry. Next time I'll add 'please'."

qa.q: What time did the district officer plan to come?
qa.a: At nine.

qa.q: What was Rukmini feeling when she read "Come to office. Now."?
qa.a: She was anxious and scared, her heart racing, sure she had made a mistake in the ration lists.

qa.q: What could Rukmini try next time a message seems harsh?
qa.a: Call or reply with a quick clarifying question before assuming she is in trouble, since short messages are often just rushed.

qa.q: How did Lokesh see his own message?
qa.a: He saw it as a rushed note typed with one thumb during a call, and didn't realise it sounded harsh until Rukmini showed him.

grounding: Shows a young adult misreading a brief text as anger when it was only rushed, and the value of checking.

subtype: Reading tone in text without voice [Interpreting]
passage: Jin had spent two evenings designing the poster for the student film society in Toronto, and at 5:40 he sent it to Felix with a long message: three colour options, two fonts, a question about the date. At 5:52 the reply came: "Fine. Use the blue." That was all. No thanks, no exclamation mark. Jin read it on the subway and felt his chest tighten. Fine? After two evenings? He drafted a reply, "Sorry it wasn't good enough," then deleted it. Instead, when he got off at his stop, he called. Felix answered on the fourth ring, breathless, wind roaring behind him. "Jin! Sorry, I'm running for a bus. The poster's great, honestly, the blue one's perfect. I'll write properly tonight." That night a message came with three exclamation marks and a list of everything he loved about it. Jin laughed at himself. The reply had been as short as Felix's free moment.

qa.q: How many colour options did Jin send?
qa.a: Three.

qa.q: What did Jin feel on reading "Fine. Use the blue."?
qa.a: Jin felt hurt and anxious, chest tightening, reading the short reply as cold after two evenings of work.

qa.q: What did Jin do instead of sending the drafted reply?
qa.a: He called Felix to check, which showed the short reply came from rushing, not displeasure.

qa.q: What was Felix's situation when he replied?
qa.a: He was running for a bus, so he typed the shortest possible answer, meaning it as approval.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult misjudging the tone of a brief message as cold, and checking with a call instead of replying to a guess.
